questions.prompt: In an n+ poly / SiO₂ / p-Si MOS capacitor, which layer stops DC current from flowing between the gate and the body?
options: The depletion region in the silicon
The SiO₂ gate oxide, an insulator
questions.explanation:
The oxide is an excellent insulator (band gap about 9 eV). So the structure is a capacitor: charge on the gate is mirrored by charge in the silicon, and no DC current flows through.
The gate is a heavily doped conductor, and the substrate is a conducting semiconductor body.

questions.prompt: An n+ poly gate sits at \(\varphi_{n^+} \approx +0.55\ \mathrm{V}\) relative to intrinsic silicon (the reader's value for degenerate n+ poly). It is on p-Si with \(N_A = 10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\). Treating the stack like a junction, the built-in potential is \(\varphi_{bi} = \varphi_{n^+} - \varphi_p\) (\(V_{th} = 26\ \mathrm{mV}\), \(n_i = 10^{10}\)). Find \(\varphi_{bi}\) in V.
questions.explanation:
\[\varphi_p = -0.026\ln(10^{7}) = -0.419\ \mathrm{V}\]
\[\varphi_{bi} = 0.55 + 0.419 \approx 0.969\ \mathrm{V}\]
The n+ gate's potential is capped near \(+0.55\ \mathrm{V}\) (its Fermi level reaches the conduction-band edge), so we don't use \(\ln(N_D/n_i)\) for degenerate doping.

questions.prompt: The flat-band voltage is \(V_{FB} = -\varphi_{bi}\) (no oxide charge). For an n+ poly gate (\(\varphi_{n^+} = +0.55\ \mathrm{V}\)) on p-Si with \(N_A = 5\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), find \(V_{FB}\) in V.
questions.explanation:
\(V_{FB}\) is the gate voltage that cancels the built-in potential, which leaves the bands flat and no charge anywhere:
\[\varphi_p = -0.026\ln(5\times10^{6}) = -0.401\ \mathrm{V},\quad V_{FB} = -(0.55 + 0.401) \approx -0.951\ \mathrm{V}\]
Negative: at \(V_{GB} = 0\) the p-surface is already somewhat depleted. (The reader's worked example quotes \(-0.952\ \mathrm{V}\); with these constants it comes out to \(-0.951\ \mathrm{V}\). That's a rounding difference.)

questions.prompt: At \(V_{GB} = 0\), an n+ poly gate on p-Si is connected through the external wire. Which way does charge settle?
options: No charge anywhere; zero volts means flat bands
The silicon surface becomes depleted (negative acceptor charge) and the gate holds a matching positive charge, because the gate's Fermi level was higher
questions.explanation:
As in a pn junction, electrons flow from the n+ gate (high Fermi level) to the p body until the Fermi levels line up. That leaves the gate positive and the surface depleted. A built-in potential \(\varphi_{bi}\) drops across the oxide plus the silicon.
To get flat bands you must apply \(V_{GB} = V_{FB} = -\varphi_{bi} < 0\).

questions.prompt: A high-k dielectric with \(\varepsilon_r = 10\) and thickness 2 nm replaces SiO₂. What is its 'equivalent oxide thickness' (the SiO₂ thickness with the same \(C_{ox}\)), in nm?
questions.explanation:
\[C = \frac{\varepsilon_{hk}}{t_{hk}} = \frac{\varepsilon_{SiO_2}}{EOT} \Rightarrow EOT = t_{hk}\frac{3.9}{10} = 0.78\ \mathrm{nm}\]
Gotcha: a thicker film gives MORE capacitance than a thin SiO₂ layer. The physical thickness limits gate leakage (tunnelling), while the EOT sets the electrical behaviour.

questions.prompt: For a p+ poly gate (\(\varphi_{p^+} \approx -0.55\ \mathrm{V}\)) on n-type silicon (\(N_D = 10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\)), what is \(\varphi_{bi} = \varphi_{gate} - \varphi_{body}\), in V?
questions.explanation:
\[\varphi_n = +0.026\ln10^{6} = 0.359\ \mathrm{V}\]
\[\varphi_{bi} = -0.55 - 0.359 \approx -0.909\ \mathrm{V}\]
Gotcha: the sign flips compared with n+/p (so \(V_{FB} = +0.909\ \mathrm{V}\)), and \(\varphi_{bi}\) is not just \(\varphi_{p^+}\).

questions.prompt: A student says: 'Since the oxide is an insulator, the MOS capacitor's gate voltage can't affect the silicon underneath.' What's the error?
options: Nothing; the gate controls only the oxide
The field passes through the insulator: gate charge induces an equal and opposite charge in the silicon, and that charge changes the carrier concentrations at the surface
Current tunnels through even thick oxides, which is how the gate works
The gate only affects the silicon if it's metal, not poly
questions.explanation:
An insulator blocks current, not electric fields. By Gauss's law, gate charge \(Q_G\) is balanced by \(-Q_G\) in the silicon: holes (accumulation), ionised acceptors (depletion) or electrons (inversion).
This 'field effect' is what makes the MOSFET work.

questions.prompt: Preview of the MOSFET: adding n+ source and drain regions on either side of the MOS capacitor's gate turns it into an NMOS transistor. Why does that only conduct once the surface is inverted?
options: Inversion forms an n-type electron channel at the surface that connects the n+ source to the n+ drain; otherwise they're separated by p-type silicon (back-to-back diodes)
The source and drain conduct through the oxide
Accumulation is what forms the channel
The p-substrate conducts between them at any gate voltage
questions.explanation:
n+ / p / n+ without a channel is two pn junctions back to back, so no current flows. Inversion puts electrons under the gate, giving a continuous n path.
The gate voltage at which that happens is the threshold voltage \(V_T\) (the vt skill).

questions.prompt: Preview of gate capacitance: a MOSFET gate is \(W = 1\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) wide and \(L = 0.1\ \mu\mathrm{m}\) long, with \(t_{ox} = 2\ \mathrm{nm}\). What is \(C_{ox}WL\), in fF?
questions.explanation:
\[C_{ox} = 17.25\ \mathrm{fF/\mu m^2},\quad WL = 0.1\ \mu\mathrm{m^2} \Rightarrow C = 1.73\ \mathrm{fF}\]
Tiny capacitances like this, times how many gates switch, set digital speed and power (\(CV^2f\)).

questions.prompt: Preview of gate material: changing an n+ poly gate to a p+ poly gate on the same p-Si body changes \(\varphi_{gate}\) from \(+0.55\) to \(-0.55\ \mathrm{V}\). By how much does \(V_{FB}\) (and therefore \(V_T\)) shift, in V?
questions.explanation:
\[\Delta V_{FB} = -\Delta\varphi_{gate} = -(-0.55 - 0.55) = +1.1\ \mathrm{V}\]
About a band gap. Gate material is a major knob for setting threshold voltages.
